## Instructions for Snow

The first flake arrives without announcement. It is small, tentative, a single white punctuation mark against the grey. You might miss it if you are looking at your phone. You might miss it if you are thinking about tomorrow. You might miss it if you are doing the dishes, or composing an email in your head, or rehearsing a conversation that happened three years ago. But if you happen to be looking out the window at that exact moment, you will feel something shift. A tiny, almost imperceptible pull. The world has decided to change its texture.

I have always been susceptible to this pull. It is why I find it difficult to get anything done in winter. The moment the first flake appears, I become useless. I stand at the window like a dog watching a door, except the door is the whole sky. I should be working. I have deadlines, chores, obligations. Yet the snow has a way of making all of that feel laughably small. It is a quiet kind of rebellion: the snow falls, and the world stops pretending it is important.

There is a sound to snow, though we rarely talk about it. Before the snow arrives, the air itself seems to change. It becomes softer, more padded. Sound waves travel differently through a falling curtain of moisture, and there is a hush that comes over the landscape, as if the earth has pressed a finger to its lips. The poet William Carlos Williams noticed this. He wrote about how a field of snow looks like the sky turned upside down, but I think he missed the more important thing. Snow is not just a visual event. It is an acoustic event. It is the closest thing we have to silence made visible.

On the first day of a snowfall, the silence is still incomplete. You can hear the occasional crunch of boots, the distant rumble of a car, the drip of melting flakes from the eaves. But by the second day, after the snow has had time to settle, the world acquires a muffled quality. It is like walking through an anechoic chamber, a room designed to absorb all sound. In such a chamber, the sound of your own heartbeat can become unbearable. But outside, in the snow, the quiet is gentler. It does not force you to confront your own machinery. It simply asks you to lower your voice.

When I was a child, snow meant a phone call in the predawn darkness. My mother would answer, speak in low tones, and then turn to us with that particular look of ill-concealed joy. No school. We would erupt from our beds, wrap ourselves in layers of insufficient clothing, and tumble out into the white. There was a seriousness to childhood snow play that adults have forgotten. Building a fort was not just a game. It was a matter of life and death, or at least of territory. We would pack snow into rectangular blocks, stack them with desperate precision, and then declare ourselves kings of a frozen kingdom. There were snowball wars, of course, but those were sacred rituals, governed by elaborate rules of engagement. You never threw a snowball at someone’s head. You never packed it so hard it became ice. You always gave a warning shout before the volley.

I remember the particular texture of snow in my mittens. It would melt slowly against the wool, then refreeze into small crystalline clumps, and by the end of the afternoon my hands would be wet, red, and numb. The cold had a way of making the body feel invisible. I would stand in the middle of the yard, arms outstretched, and imagine that I was not really there at all. The snow would fall through me, and I would be nothing but a pair of eyes floating above the ground. That is what snow does. It invites you to dissolve.

Now I am an adult, and snow has become a different kind of event. It is no longer an excuse for joy but an inconvenience, a complication in the logistics of living. The weather app alerts me to an incoming storm. I buy bread and milk with the rest of the anxious hive. I dig out my car, scrape the windshield, leave a geometric pattern of tracks in the driveway. The magic is still there, but it requires an effort to access. I have to consciously choose to stand still in the cold, to let the snow land on my hair, to feel the particular hush that was once the background of my entire winter existence.

Why do we have to choose? Why does wonder become so difficult? The answer, I think, has something to do with attention. We are bombarded with information, with stimulus, with the constant low-grade hum of productivity. Our minds are rarely empty. They are filled with to-do lists, with anxieties, with the mental residue of social media feeds. The snow is a counterpoint to this. It asks for nothing. It expects nothing. It simply falls, indifferent to our schedules and our worries. To watch the snow is to practice a form of attention that our culture no longer values. It is to be present, without agenda, in the presence of something beautiful and unstoppable.

I have a theory about why snow makes us quiet. It is not just the sound absorption of the snow itself. It is not just the cold. It is that snow is a visible representation of a larger truth: the world is going to do what it is going to do, regardless of our plans. The snow does not ask permission. It falls when the conditions are right, and it stops when they are not. There is something profoundly reassuring about this. It relieves us of the burden of control. For a few hours, we are not expected to fix anything. We are invited instead to simply watch.

And watching is a kind of participation. When we watch snow, we are not passive. We are active in a different way. Our eyes move from flake to flake, following one as it drifts, losing it, finding another. Our minds begin to slow, to sync with the rhythm of the fall. We notice the way snow collects on tree branches, first as a dusting, then as a burden. We notice the way it outlines the contours of things, softening edges, erasing distances. A fence becomes a line of white humps. A parked car becomes a rounded hill. The familiar world is transformed into something strange and beautiful, and we are here to witness it.

I remember a particular evening, several years ago, when I was walking home in the middle of a heavy snowfall. The streetlights were on, and the snow was so thick that the light seemed to be solidifying into a kind of luminous fog. There were no cars. There were no other people. There was only me and the falling snow and the sound of my boots crunching through the new layer that had accumulated on the sidewalk. I stopped in the middle of the street, under a light, and looked up. The flakes came directly into my eyes, and I let them. I must have stood there for a minute, maybe two. It felt like an eternity. I felt an enormous sense of peace, a kind of emptiness that was not a void but a relief. It was as if the snow was washing away all the accumulated noise of my life, all the half-formed thoughts, all the unfinished conversations. I was just a person standing in the dark, receiving the sky.

There is a term in Japanese culture: yūgen. It is often translated as "a profound, mysterious sense of the beauty of the universe" or "the deep and mysterious feeling of the beauty of things." It is not a feeling you can manufacture. It arises when you are confronted with something so vast and so beyond your comprehension that you feel simultaneously insignificant and connected. Snow is a gateway to yūgen. It is a small thing, a frozen water crystal, but when it falls in its billions, it becomes something else entirely. It becomes a landscape, a mood, a metaphor. It becomes a blanket that covers the world and reveals its true shape.

In Zen, there is a saying: "Before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. After enlightenment, chop wood, carry water." The snow reminds me of this. It is not a special occasion. It is just winter, doing what winter does. And yet, if you pay attention, it is the most special occasion you have ever witnessed. The ordinary becomes extraordinary not because it changes, but because you finally see it. The snow is the same snow it has always been. I am the same person I have always been. But for a moment, in the act of watching, the boundary between the two dissolves.

I think this is why snow appears so often in literature. It is a perfect narrative device, a blank page on which the story can be written. It is also a perfect symbol of the mind, particularly the meditative mind. The snow falls, and the world becomes quiet, and in that quiet we can hear ourselves thinking. The psychologist and philosopher William James called the stream of consciousness a "buzzing, blooming confusion." But snow is the opposite. It is a stream that has slowed to a crawl, a blooming that has been leached of all color. It is a way of clearing the mind by subtraction.

When I write, I often think of snow. Not because my writing is white, but because I want it to have the same quality of inevitability. A good sentence, like a snowflake, should feel as if it could not have been otherwise. It should fall exactly where it is supposed to fall, and it should land with a certain quiet precision. Of course, this is an illusion. A snowflake is a complex structure, the result of temperature, humidity, and chance. A sentence is the result of effort, revision, and luck. But the illusion is worth pursuing. The goal is to make the reader feel that the words were not manufactured but discovered, that they were there all along, falling out of the sky, waiting to be caught.

There is a particular joy in being the first person to walk through fresh snow. The surface is unbroken, a smooth white expanse. Your boot sinks in, and you leave a dark, definite mark. The track behind you is a record of your passage, a line of footprints leading from here to there. But within a few hours, the snow will fill in those footprints. The marks will soften, fade, and eventually disappear, as if you were never there. This, too, is a lesson. We are temporary. Our effects on the world are temporary. The snow is honest about this, in a way that most things are not. It does not promise permanence. It does not cling. It falls, it covers, it melts. It is gone.

And yet, the memory of a snowfall persists. I can remember weather from decades ago with a vividness that I cannot muster for most of my own life. I remember the snow that fell on the day my grandfather died. I remember the snow that fell on the night of my high school graduation, a freak spring storm that turned the ceremonial grounds into a surreal white landscape. I remember the snow that fell when I was in the hospital, after my daughter was born, and how I watched it through the fourth-floor window while she slept in a clear plastic bassinet. Each of those snowfalls is etched into me, not because the snow was special, but because I was paying attention. The snow gave me an excuse to stop, to be present, to mark the moment with a kind of reverence that I otherwise would have lacked.

There is a concept called "choiceless awareness," from the spiritual teacher Jiddu Krishnamurti. It refers to a state of observation without preference or judgment. You simply see what is, without labeling it good or bad, without wanting it to be different. Snow is the perfect teacher of choiceless awareness. You cannot argue with the snow. You cannot negotiate with it. It falls, and you either accept it or you spend the day in a state of quiet resentment. Acceptance is the easier path. It is also the more beautiful one. When you stop trying to control the snow, you can begin to enjoy it.

I have been sitting at my desk for over an hour now, writing about snow, while the real snow falls outside my window. I have been aware of it in my peripheral vision, a steady white drift, a thickening layer on the railing of the balcony. The room has grown darker. The temperature has dropped, and I can see my breath faintly when I sigh. I should go out. I should put on my coat and my boots and walk to the park at the end of the street. The park is a large open field, and on a day like this it will be empty. I will be the only one there, standing in the middle of all that white, and the snow will fall on me, and the world will be hushed.

I think about how many snowfalls I have missed. I think about all the years I spent rushing through winter, head down, phone in hand, eager to get from one heated building to another. I think about all the flakes that have fallen without being seen, all the silence that has gone unheard. There is a kind of grief in this, but it is a gentle grief. It is the grief of a person who has finally learned to stand still, and who knows that there will never be enough time to make up for the standing still that was never done.

But grief, like snow, can be beautiful. It can be a soft, cold instruction. It can teach you to slow down. It can teach you to open your eyes and look at what is actually in front of you. Tonight, when the snow stops falling and the clouds clear, I will look up at the stars. They will be sharper than usual, because the air will be clean and the snow will reflect the moonlight. The world will be bright, even in the dark. And I will be grateful, the way you are grateful for a gift you did not know you needed, then discover you cannot live without.

This is my instruction for snow. Do not miss it. Do not treat it as an inconvenience. If you can, take a break from whatever you are doing. Stand by the window. Go outside. Turn your face to the sky. Let the flakes land on your cheeks and eyelashes. Listen to the hush. Remember that you are small, and that this is not a tragedy. It is a relief. The world is larger than you, and it is falling all around you, and it is beautiful. For a while, you do not need to do anything. You only need to watch. The snow will do the rest. It will cover the ground. It will soften the edges. It will quiet the noise. It will give you a moment of grace, and then it will melt. But you will have seen it. You will have been present. And that is enough.
